Upbraid

/up-BRAYD/ - rhymes with parade · verb

Hear It

What It Means

Upbraid means to criticize or scold severely.

The head librarian upbraided the volunteers for shelving by color, and the lecture outlasted the mistake by an hour.

Worked Example

After the third overdrawn month, Dana's grandmother upbraided her across the Sunday roast — an itemized scolding that began with the coffee habit and ended, somehow, with the unused gym membership.

To upbraid is to scold with the receipts out: severe, specific, and aimed at a fault the scolder can name. It is sterner than criticize and more thorough than snap. Within this unit, vituperate goes further — abuse for its own sake — while a scathing remark wounds without the sermon.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

scold: the everyday word for angry correction

reprimand: an official scolding, often on the record

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

praise: to name what someone did well

commend: to single someone out for approval

Where it sits · how harsh the dressing-down gets — scold → upbraid → excoriate

scold vs. upbraid: Scold is milder than upbraid — quicker, hotter, and over by dinner.

excoriate vs. upbraid: Excoriate is fiercer than upbraid: an upbraiding is a severe telling-off, while to excoriate is to take the hide off entirely.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — up-

Prefix — up-: up (Old English)

Root — braid

Root — braid: to pull, to twist, to brandish (Old English bregdan)

Put it together

Put it together: Up- (up) + braid (to pull, to twist — Old English bregdan) = to pull up. To upbraid someone was originally to 'pull up' a fault and brandish it in their face; the same twisting verb, gone domestic, gave us the braid — hair pulled and twisted into rope.

Use the root in a new word: braid

Use the root in a new word: braid: She learned to braid her sister's hair into a fishtail — three strands pulled and twisted tight.

Word Choice

formal / literary

Upbraid is the writer's word for a severe, pointed scolding — someone in authority pulling a fault into the light. Scold is its kitchen-table cousin; reprimand puts it on official paper. When the scolding curdles into a stream of abuse, this unit's vituperate takes over.
